summary: All 16 saved objects and all 28 English flow paragraphs were read against the current Chinese edition and faithful source prose. Scientific qualifications and the three registered endpoint corrections are retained. Two local explanations need clarification for independent eight-year-old reading: saturation mass and the higher-temperature endpoint comparison. This is a new English text review, not recovered historical approval or a figure/display/accessibility release.

contentDesign.jobStory: When I read this physics lesson on my own, I want to understand why squeezing a gas can turn it into liquid without changing pressure, so I can follow the isotherm from vapor to liquid.
contentDesign.evidence: The charter names an eight-year-old independent self-learner; N38's source explains the compression experiment, its isotherm and saturated vapor. No actual reader interview or reading-session evidence was collected.
contentDesign.questionItShouldAnswer: Why can pressure stay the same while a gas is compressed and becomes liquid?
contentDesign.questionItAnswersNow: The pressure plateau is caused by condensation at fixed temperature during pure-substance liquid-vapor coexistence, not by compressing a fixed mass of vapor without changing it.

paragraphAssessments.observation: Retains the objective of studying pressure and volume to understand forward and reverse phase changes; does not turn boiling observation into a sufficient explanation.

The cylinder is closed, total mass fixed and substance pure. The chosen below-critical temperature must permit liquid-vapor equilibrium; this is not a claim that every subcritical state is already two-phase.

Work transfers energy into the substance, but heat exchanged also determines its internal-energy change. The source's unconditional compression-increases-internal-energy claim is not carried into the learner explanation.

The maintained-temperature liquid bath and slow compression provide heat exchange. Energy released during compression and condensation can leave; constant temperature is not confused with no heat transfer.
Boyle-Mariotte behavior is approximate and restricted to dilute gas at constant temperature. Real-gas deviation precedes the equilibrium condensation plateau.
The transparent-liquid observation is attributed to the textbook, and condensation is identified as a gas-to-liquid change. No invented measurement is supplied.
Liquid gains exactly the mass lost by vapor during slow fixed-temperature compression; total mass remains unchanged.
The pressure plateau ends when vapor has condensed completely. Changing phase masses and volumes are not described as creating or destroying matter.
The steep liquid branch follows condensation completion. Low compressibility is distinguished from absolute incompressibility.
Defines an isotherm with T, then P and V in the source order. V is total volume of fixed total mass, including both phases when present.
V2 is condensation onset and V1 completion. The V greater-than-or-equal-to V2 vapor interval retains the source expression.
Read with the preceding inequality, equality refers to V2 and the saturated-vapor boundary. The V less-than V1 liquid interval is unchanged.
The interval between endpoints contains both phases; total volume is not the volume of an unchanged mass of vapor.
Similar isotherms for other substances are limited to below-critical states permitting coexistence, rather than every temperature or phase.
Compression reduces total volume from V2 to V1 while pressure stays constant and vapor becomes liquid.
B-A identifies the plateau; endpoint language allows the limit where one phase just appears or disappears.
Phase masses stay steady with time at one fixed-temperature, fixed-volume equilibrium point but can differ at another point. Molecules still leave and return.
Average evaporation and condensation rates balance over equal times; microscopic motion does not stop. This explains equilibrium dynamically.
The saturated-vapor definition and equilibrium mass statement are sound, but 'vapor-phase volume' and 'corresponding saturation mass' do not explain the amount in child-readable terms.
The apparent maximum is an equilibrium statement, not a prohibition on a short-lived excess before condensation restores equilibrium.
p0 is saturated vapor pressure. Volume independence is restricted to the pure substance at fixed temperature with both phases coexisting, and explicitly withdrawn beyond that scope.
Condensation permits volume reduction because equal mass occupies much less volume as liquid; no fixed-vapor-mass pressure law is asserted.
A small transient increase in vapor density and pressure disturbs equilibrium; returning molecules then outnumber escaping molecules.
Net condensation restores the earlier equilibrium vapor density and pressure only while temperature is unchanged and both phases remain.
Vapor mass decreases as it condenses. The result is expressly not a claim about pressure staying unchanged when a fixed mass of vapor alone is compressed.

Same CO2 mass, higher but still subcritical constant temperature and dilute ideal-gas approximation are retained. Corrected onset V2-prime less-than V2 is present; the prime mark needs a local verbal link to this second curve.

Corrected completion V1-prime greater-than V1 compares liquid endpoints at different temperatures. 'Further compression to' attaches that comparison to motion along one curve and can look like increasing volume.
The liquid-filled endpoint is correctly V1-prime, with the earlier subscript convention preserved. No critical-point calculation or N39 task is added.

findings.quote: At a given temperature and vapor-phase volume, the equilibrium vapor has the corresponding saturation mass.
findings.readerConfusion: I can read the definition of saturated vapor, but what space is 'vapor-phase volume', and what does 'corresponding saturation mass' tell me about how much vapor can stay there? Neither expression is explained by that sentence.
findings.focusedRemedy: Keep the saturated-vapor definition and the following non-equilibrium qualification. Replace only the next two sentences with a concrete explanation of fixed vapor space, fixed temperature, the equilibrium amount and excess vapor condensing.
findings.suggestedReplacementForQuotedSentenceAnd:
For a fixed temperature, a fixed space occupied by vapor holds a certain mass of vapor in equilibrium with the liquid.
If that same space temporarily contains extra vapor at the same temperature, the extra vapor condenses into liquid until equilibrium returns.
findings.scienceGuardrails: Do not make this an absolute ban on transient excess vapor, confuse vapor space with the cylinder's total volume, or imply a universal mass independent of temperature and volume. This is explanation of the current Chinese meaning, not new data.
findings.anchorRemedy: Derive the affected anchor again from the revised saved flow; do not hand-count paragraph positions.

findings.readerConfusion: Compression has meant making volume smaller. This greater-than sign now looks as though I must make volume larger to finish. The prose also has not explicitly said that the prime mark labels endpoints on the higher-temperature curve.
findings.focusedRemedy: Locally identify the prime mark as the higher-temperature endpoint label. Separate decreasing volume along that curve from comparing its liquid endpoint with the lower-temperature endpoint. Keep every registered formula, sign, original, reason and binding unchanged.
findings.suggestedReplacementForFlowParagraph26:
Keep decreasing the volume until condensation is complete.
The liquid-end volume is larger than for the lower-temperature curve: $V_1'>V_1$.
The isotherm then becomes steep.
findings.scienceGuardrails: Retain V2-prime<V2, V1-prime>V1 and the final V1-prime in their existing order. Do not flip the inequality, redefine V1/V2, invent a measurement or add an unregistered mathematical expression. No Figure 55 or shared N39 edit is required.
findings.recheckScope: Only the revised explanation and its resulting flow/bindings need follow-up; do not redo unrelated source, science or figure PASS stages.

records.assessment: Uses the established vapor-onset family V2. At higher subcritical temperature, the same mass has the smaller vapor endpoint.
Uses the established liquid-end family V1. Its larger higher-temperature endpoint is a comparison between curves, not an increase along compression.
The liquid-filled state is the condensation-completion endpoint V1-prime.
